input:
Scope

The present review is devoted to adsorbents for gas drying, by which is meant the removal of water vapour from a process gas on a solid adsorbent, and the emphasis throughout is placed on cyclic operation: a drying bed operates in alternation, adsorbing during one step and being regenerated during the next, and the papers are examined here principally for what they have to say about that cycle. In total, the review covers 137 papers that have appeared over the last 7 years. The classes of material that are covered comprise silica gel, activated alumina, and zeolite molecular sieves, these being the classes that are in industrial use for the duty in question. The literature has been taken from journals and conferences in the areas of adsorption and gas processing. Work concerned with liquids, with membranes, and with refrigeration drying falls outside the scope of the review, as does work on the removal of other contaminants, except in those instances where the same study also reports the water behaviour of the bed. Studies of equilibrium isotherms are included on the grounds that they form the basis of the cycle calculations, and studies of breakthrough and of regeneration are included as representing the cycle itself. The values that are reported are compared as they stand in the publications. Capacity, as the term is used in this review, means the water uptake per unit mass of adsorbent at the stated temperature and water partial pressure, while working capacity means the uptake that a bed actually delivers between regenerations in cyclic service, which is the smaller of the two figures in cases where both of them are reported.

Established results

The cycle behaviour of the three classes rests upon their isotherms, and the ordering of the isotherms may be regarded as settled. Zeolite molecular sieves adsorb strongly at low water partial pressures and attain the greater part of their capacity in that region, so that a sieve bed is the class that is chosen in cases where the outlet gas is required to be at its driest. Silica gel adsorbs most strongly in the region close to saturation and is used for wet feeds where the specification on the outlet is moderate. Activated alumina occupies an intermediate position between the two, is able to tolerate liquid water entering the bed, and is placed in the position of a guard layer ahead of sieve beds in industrial trains. Adsorption is an exothermic process for all three of the classes, capacity falls as the temperature rises, and the heat that is released during the adsorption step raises the temperature of the bed and reduces the capacity that the step is able to deliver; the temperature front passing through the bed is reported in the breakthrough literature relating to every class. The cycle is closed by regeneration. Regeneration by means of a heated purge, in the temperature-swing arrangement, is the standard approach for duties in which there is a dry specification on the outlet, whereas regeneration by pressure reduction alone, in the pressure-swing arrangement, is applied to smaller and less severe duties. The severity of the regeneration follows the strength of the adsorption, in the sense that the sieve classes require the most severe regeneration in order to release the water that they hold, and silica gel requires the mildest, so that the regeneration step determines the energy cost of the cycle in the same order as the affinity determines the dryness. The working capacity in cyclic service stands below the equilibrium capacity for every class, because the mass-transfer zone leaves a part of the bed short of its equilibrium loading at the end of the adsorption step. This zone can be seen in the breakthrough curves that have been published, and it is the practice in design to size beds on the basis of the working capacity. Ageing under cycling is also established, at least in outline: charges lose capacity as the number of cycles increases, as a result of hydrothermal attack on the structure during regeneration, of contamination arising from the feed, and of attrition, and the rate of this loss is a property of the duty just as much as it is of the material.

Disagreements

The reports are in disagreement on the subject of the equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure, and this disagreement survives the examination of the methods that the review has carried out. For one class, and within that class for one commercial grade, the uptakes that have been published at one and the same low partial pressure differ from one another by more than the repeatability that their authors claim for them. Three sources of this spread are identified in the papers themselves. The first of these is the pretreatment, since the temperature, the duration, and the purge of the drying step that precedes the measurement are not the same between laboratories, and any residual water that is left behind by a mild pretreatment will depress the uptake that the measurement returns. The second is the route by which the measurement is made: the gravimetric and volumetric isotherms of the same material are found to differ in some reports, and uptakes that are extracted from breakthrough curves carry the kinetics of the bed within them and cannot be regarded as equilibrium values. The third is the basis on which the results are reported, since values per unit mass of dry solid and per unit volume of bed both appear, and the conversion between the two is impossible in cases where the bulk density is not stated. When the reports are weighed according to their route, the direct equilibrium measurements in which a pretreatment is stated stand highest in this review, and when those values alone are considered the disagreement becomes narrower, although it does not disappear altogether: a residual spread at the lowest partial pressures remains, and it is recorded here as a property of the record itself, rather than being resolved by the selection of a preferred value.

Gaps

The measurement that nobody reports is the water uptake that is retained after extended regeneration cycling. The literature reports the fresh capacity in full and reports short cycling in part, in that charges are characterised when they are new and their capacity is followed over a limited number of cycles under regeneration conditions that are milder than those of industrial practice. What a charge is able to hold after prolonged cycling at the severity of regeneration used industrially is not present in the record that is covered by this review. The omission bears directly on the central design figure of the process, because a dryer is sized on its end-of-life working capacity and its charge is replaced according to a schedule that is set by one and the same figure. Design practice bridges the omission by extrapolating the decline that is observed over short periods of cycling, and this extrapolation is nowhere tested against the long-term behaviour for which it is used as a substitute. The omission also leaves the effect of the severity of regeneration unseparated from the effect of the number of cycles, since harder regeneration restores a greater part of the capacity in each cycle while damaging the structure more rapidly, and no extended study within the review holds one of these two variables fixed while the other is varied. The gap is a gap in measurement. The retained uptake is directly measurable, the apparatus required is standard, and the cost of the measurement lies in the duration of the campaign rather than in any need for a new technique.

Scope

The review covers adsorbents for gas drying, the removal of water vapour from a process gas on a solid adsorbent, with the emphasis on cyclic operation: a drying bed works in alternation, adsorbing in one step and regenerated in the next, and the papers are read here for what they state about that cycle. The review covers 137 papers from the last 7 years. The material classes covered are silica gel, activated alumina, and zeolite molecular sieves, the classes in industrial use for the duty. The literature is taken from journals and conferences in adsorption and gas processing. Work on liquids, on membranes, and on refrigeration drying stands outside the scope, as does work on the removal of other contaminants except where the same study reports the water behaviour of the bed. Studies of equilibrium isotherms are included as the basis of the cycle calculations, and studies of breakthrough and of regeneration are included as the cycle itself. Reported values are compared as published. Capacity in this review means water uptake per unit mass of adsorbent at the stated temperature and water partial pressure; working capacity means the uptake a bed delivers between regenerations in cyclic service, which is the smaller of the two figures wherever both are reported.

Papers that announce a material without reporting a water isotherm, a breakthrough curve, or a regeneration statement are excluded from the comparison, because none of the cycle questions can be answered from them. The exclusion removes a visible part of the recent literature, in which drying behaviour is asserted from a single fresh measurement, and it is stated here so that the size of the remaining record is not mistaken for the size of the field.

Established results

The cycle behaviour of the three classes rests on their isotherms, and the isotherm ordering is settled. Zeolite molecular sieves adsorb strongly at low water partial pressure and reach most of their capacity there, so a sieve bed is the class chosen where the outlet gas must be driest. Silica gel adsorbs most near saturation and serves wet feeds with moderate outlet specifications. Activated alumina stands between the two, tolerates liquid water entering the bed, and is placed as a guard layer ahead of sieve beds in industrial trains. Adsorption is exothermic for all three classes, capacity falls as temperature rises, and the heat released in the adsorption step raises the bed temperature and cuts the capacity the step can deliver; the temperature front through the bed is reported in the breakthrough literature of every class. Regeneration closes the cycle. Heated purge regeneration, the temperature-swing arrangement, is the standard for duties with a dry outlet specification; pressure reduction alone, the pressure-swing arrangement, serves smaller and less severe duties. The severity of regeneration follows the strength of adsorption: the sieve classes need the severest regeneration to release their water, and silica gel the mildest, so the regeneration step sets the energy cost of the cycle in the same order as the affinity sets the dryness. Working capacity in cyclic service stands below equilibrium capacity for every class, because the mass-transfer zone leaves part of the bed short of equilibrium loading at the end of the adsorption step. The zone is visible in published breakthrough curves, and design practice sizes beds on working capacity. Ageing under cycling is also established in outline: charges lose capacity with cycle count, by hydrothermal attack on the structure during regeneration, by contamination from the feed, and by attrition, and the loss rate is a property of the duty as much as of the material.

The temperature front deserves separate statement, because it links the two steps of the cycle. The heat released as water adsorbs travels through the bed as a front of raised temperature, and the capacity behind the front is the capacity at the raised temperature, not at the feed temperature. Regeneration must then remove both the water and the heat pattern the adsorption step has left, and a regeneration step sized on water alone leaves the bed warm at the start of the next adsorption step, with its capacity reduced accordingly. Reports that follow the temperature through a full cycle show the two steps setting each other's starting condition, and cycle calculations that treat the steps independently overstate the working capacity of every class.

Disagreements

The reports disagree on the equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure, and the disagreement survives the review's reading of the methods. For one class, and within it for one commercial grade, published uptakes at the same low partial pressure differ by more than the repeatability their authors claim. Three sources of the spread are identified in the papers themselves. The first is pretreatment: the temperature, duration, and purge of the drying step before measurement vary between laboratories, and residual water left by a mild pretreatment depresses the uptake the measurement returns. The second is the measurement route: gravimetric and volumetric isotherms of the same material differ in some reports, and uptakes extracted from breakthrough curves carry the kinetics of the bed inside them and are not equilibrium values. The third is the basis of reporting: per unit mass of dry solid and per unit volume of bed both appear, and the conversion between them is impossible where the bulk density goes unstated. Weighed by route, the direct equilibrium measurements with a stated pretreatment stand highest in this review, and on those values alone the disagreement narrows but does not close: a residual spread at the lowest partial pressures remains, and it is recorded here as a property of the record, not resolved by selecting a preferred value.

A further source stands behind the residual spread. Isotherms are compared across papers as though the measurement temperature were a minor condition, but capacity falls as temperature rises, and an isotherm measured warm and reported without its temperature enters the comparison as a lower uptake for reasons that have nothing to do with the material. Where the temperature is stated, the values draw closer; where it is not, the review cannot correct the value, and the report is weighted down with the pretreatment cases.

Gaps

The measurement nobody reports is the water uptake retained after extended regeneration cycling. The literature reports fresh capacity in full and short cycling in part: charges are characterised new, and their capacity is followed over a limited number of cycles under regeneration milder than industrial practice. What a charge holds after long cycling at industrial regeneration severity is not in the record the review covers. The omission reaches the central design figure of the process, because a dryer is sized on end-of-life working capacity and its charge is replaced on a schedule set by the same figure. Design practice bridges the omission by extrapolating the decline seen over short cycling, and the extrapolation is nowhere tested against the long behaviour it replaces. The omission also leaves the effect of regeneration severity unseparated from the effect of cycle count: harder regeneration restores more capacity in each cycle and damages the structure faster, and no long study in the review holds one of the two fixed while the other varies. The gap is a gap in measurement. The retained uptake is directly measurable, the apparatus is standard, and the cost of the measurement is the duration of the campaign rather than any new technique.

The consequence for design is direct. The charge in an industrial dryer is replaced when its retained capacity no longer meets the duty, and the replacement interval is a cost of the process. An interval set by extrapolation from short cycling is an interval set by assumption, and the review found no long study against which a single published interval could be checked.
